source.title: Latent Speech-Text Transformer
source.authors: Yen-Ju Lu; Yashesh Gaur; Wei Zhou; Benjamin Muller; J. Villalba; N. Dehak; Luke S. Zettlemoyer; Gargi Ghosh; Mike Lewis; Srinivas Iyer; Duc-Cuong Le

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present and usable; minor text-extraction artifacts do not prevent reading.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports downstream benchmark performance across model scales in speech-text models, extending scale-related evaluation to a new modality and training setting.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior scaling-law work and refers to a scaling-law optimum, but does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss or fit power laws. Rows below are its own HellaSwag accuracy results across model scales. Other reported benchmark and transfer results do not compare scales.
record.test_reason: This is a method paper. It borrows the Hoffmann et al. 20× tokens-per-parameter rule to set training budgets, then reports how its LST architecture compares with a SpeechLLM baseline at several sizes. It fits no power law, measures no held-out loss against scale, and does not examine whether downstream accuracy is predictable from scale or loss. The scale rows report LST-vs-baseline gaps (own method vs comparator), not a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that LST improves speech and text story-completion accuracy over SpeechLLM baselines in both compute- and data-controlled settings, while shortening sequences and cutting compute. They say its gains grow with scale from 420M to 1.8B and persist at 7B under fixed-token budgets, which they read as more favourable compute-optimal scaling for spoken language modelling.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares downstream HellaSwag accuracy across model sizes in speech-text models; it does not measure held-out cross-entropy or fit scaling-law curves.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports results in both compute-optimal and fixed-token settings, and separately for S→S and T→T.

fits_no_version.finding: LST's HellaSwag advantage over the baseline widens from 420M to 1.8B under near compute-optimal training: S→S gap grows from 0.8 to 3.7 points. Under a fixed token budget the gap narrows from 1B to 7B (4.5 to 2.2) but persists.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compressing speech tokens into latent patches improves the downstream scaling behaviour of speech-text language models relative to token-level baselines.

record.problems: For the scaling results, the text reports selected sizes and benchmark accuracies, not a fitted performance curve or prospective prediction. Uncertainty is not reported for these specific scale comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out. Other benchmark results are not reported as scale comparisons; cited scaling-law results are not this study's own results.

untested.parts: No held-out loss measured against parameters, tokens or compute.
No fits, so no extrapolation is tested.
The Chinchilla 20× ratio is adopted as a training recipe; the optimum is not tested.
No study of depth or width at fixed parameter count.
Speech-text setting, but no power-law form is fitted.
Accuracy rises with size at only a few points. Predictability, or any relation to loss, is not analysed.
No analysis of exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader labelled this as testing V6 with supports. I reject that. The study uses the Chinchilla allocation as a tool, and its scale results are its own method versus a baseline. Baseline accuracy does rise with size (e.g. S→S 28.4→35.3 from 420M to 1.8B), but that is a few points with no forecast, fit or loss relation, so it cannot bear on 'predictable' improvement. The 7B run is deliberately below the token optimum.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No power-law fit or prediction from small runs to larger runs.
No comparison of loss-minimizing parameter and token allocations across compute budgets.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study examines speech-text training but does not test whether a power-law form for loss holds in this or other modalities or regimes.
Reports HellaSwag accuracy at selected model sizes, but does not fit or evaluate forecasts, or relate performance to pretraining loss.
No analysis of loss-law exponents, fitting choices, or departures from a single power law.
